Looking at the actual workflow setup, SIT Gate runs automated checks on release branches and only deploys to SIT if those checks pass, whereas the downstream environments require explicit manual triggers.

The key difference comes down to the purpose and control model of each tier. SIT is designed as a continuous, automated integration-testing environment that should always reflect a validated build without human intervention at each step. Because there's no human in the loop making promotion decisions, the automated gate acts as that quality gatekeeper. In contrast, UAT, staging, and production are manual deployments because they're controlled by people who make explicit decisions about when and what to promote to those environments.

Human approval is already the gate for these higher tiers—through GitHub Environment protection rules requiring reviewers, plus process controls like Jira bookings and stakeholder sign-offs. An automated status check would be redundant since the real gating criteria (business approval, integration windows, release readiness) aren't things a CI check can evaluate.

The automated quality gate already ran once on the release branch at the SIT boundary, so re-running it at UAT would be pointless—what changes there is human business acceptance, not code quality. The distinction is clear: SIT uses a workflow status check as its gate, while UAT/Stage/Prod rely on GitHub Environment deployment protection rules with required reviewers. Prod and Stage are human-gated with manual triggers and likely required reviewer approvals, unlike SIT which is CI-gated and automatic. So the distinction is clear: SIT is the last automatic promotion point, while everything beyond it requires human intervention.

Human-gated deployments already have a person as the gate, so they don't need an additional CI check. Plus, SIT runs on a continuous cadence from release branch pushes for NewStore's benefit, while UAT and beyond follow the business's schedule and depend on non-code criteria like sign-offs and Jira bookings that CI can't evaluate. The manual tiers add human judgment on criteria that CI can't evaluate—business approval, integration readiness, canary validation—so they're gated by the person triggering the deployment, not by automated checks. The pattern holds: dev and SIT are automatic, so they need CI gates; test, UAT, stage, and prod are manual, so the human decision is the gate itself. Test is disposable and ungated because it's just a quick validation environment.

content.text:
Good question — and the short version is: **SIT is the last *automatic* hop, so it needs a *machine* gate. UAT (and Stage/Prod) are deliberate *human* decisions, so their gate is a *person*, not a CI check.**

## The underlying principle

Automatic promotion needs an automated gate; manual promotion already has a gate — the human clicking the button.

- **SIT deploys itself.** `deploy-sit` is triggered by the SIT Gate workflow completing (`workflow_run` + `if: conclusion == 'success'`). No human decides each SIT deploy — so something has to stand in for that judgment. That "something" is the SIT Gate. Without it, an unvalidated build would auto-flow into SIT, where NewStore runs multi-week OMS integration cycles — exactly where you don't want surprise breakage.
- **UAT/Stage/Prod are `workflow_dispatch`** — a person deliberately triggers them. That person *is* the gate, backed by process the CI literally can't evaluate.

## Why a CI gate would even be *wrong* at UAT

The entry criteria for the upper tiers aren't code-quality questions — they're things no status check can answer:

- **UAT** → "has the business signed off, per region?"
- **Stage** → "is the 2-week E2E window Jira-booked, and is NewStore's OMS SIT complete?"
- **Prod** → "release-manager approval + canary error-rate < 0.5% over 2h."

Those are human/organisational gates. They live in **GitHub Environment protection (required reviewers)** and **process**, not in a `.yml` status check.

## And the automated bar already ran once

The SIT Gate runs on the `release/**` branch. By the time you promote that branch to UAT, it has **already passed** the automated quality bar. Re-running the same checks at UAT would be redundant — what UAT *adds* is business acceptance, which is a person's call.

## So the pattern across tiers

| Tier | Trigger | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| dev | auto (push→develop) | light CI gate (contract + bundle-size) |
| **sit** | **auto (after SIT Gate)** | **full CI gate — because it's automatic** |
| test | manual | none — disposable "quick look" tier |
| uat / stage / prod | manual | **humans** — sign-off, Jira booking, Environment reviewers, canary |

So UAT isn't really "ungated" — it's **human-gated instead of CI-gated**. The automation sits at the last machine-driven hop (SIT); every hop above it is a deliberate human promotion.

(Worth noting: this is also exactly why the tag-based proposal wants immutable *tags* for those manual promotions — when a human promotes to UAT, they need to name a precise, unchanging thing to promote, not "whatever's on the branch right now.")

Found it — and it's **by design, not a permissions problem.** Vic is looking for the "Run workflow" button in the Actions UI, and that button only appears when a workflow has a **`workflow_dispatch`** trigger. Two of the six deploy workflows deliberately don't have one:

| Workflow | Trigger | Manual "Run workflow" button? |
|---|---|---|
| **deploy-dev** | `push` → `develop` only | ❌ No — auto-only |
| **deploy-sit** | `workflow_run` after **SIT Gate** passes on `release/**` | ❌ No — auto-only |
| deploy-test | `workflow_dispatch` (ref) | ✅ Yes |
| deploy-uat | `workflow_dispatch` (ref) | ✅ Yes |
| deploy-stg | `workflow_dispatch` (ref) | ✅ Yes |
| deploy-prod | `workflow_dispatch` (ref) | ✅ Yes |

So Vic can manually fire test/uat/stg/prod because those are `workflow_dispatch`. **dev and SIT have no manual trigger at all** — they're the two *automatic* tiers (this is exactly the SIT-gating design from your last question): dev deploys on every merge to `develop`, and SIT deploys only after the SIT Gate goes green on a `release/**` branch.

## How Vic actually deploys to those two

- **dev** → merge to `develop` (it deploys itself). There's no on-demand path by design.
- **SIT** → happens automatically once the **SIT Gate passes** on a release branch. Right now it *won't*, because our fresh `release/v0.1.0` gate is red (no P0 spec + no Lighthouse server). For an **out-of-band/bootstrap SIT deploy**, the documented path (05.6 Environment Details) is a **local CLI push** — `npm run push:sit` — not the Actions UI.
